opus-5.5.text:
I think the cleanest way to see it is to look at what vanilla linear attention is actually doing to its memory. You have this state, a matrix, and at every step you just add the outer product of the new key and value into it. It's purely additive. You never remove anything. So as the sequence gets longer, all these key-value associations pile on top of each other, and since the state has a fixed size, they start to interfere. When you query with a key, you get back a blurry mixture of everything you've stored. That's a big reason linear attention historically struggled on things like associative recall.

What the delta rule changes is the write operation. Before writing a new value for a key, you first read out what the memory currently predicts for that key, then you write only the difference between the target value and that prediction, scaled by a learning rate, which we call beta. So it's an error-correcting update. If the memory already stores the right thing, you barely change it. If there's an old value sitting at that key, you effectively overwrite it instead of just stacking a new one on top. It's the classic Widrow-Hoff rule from the 1960s, and it connects to Schmidhuber's fast weight programmers from the early nineties.

Another way I like to put it: the state is being trained online. At each token you take one gradient descent step on a regression loss, trying to map keys to values. Plain linear attention also corresponds to a gradient step, but on a loss that doesn't really encourage accurate retrieval. The delta rule optimizes a proper reconstruction loss. That's the conceptual leap, and it fed into this whole "test-time training" or "test-time regression" view of sequence models.

The catch was always efficiency. The update is no longer a simple sum, so it looked inherently sequential, and people assumed it couldn't be trained in parallel on GPUs at scale. A lot of my work was showing that you can parallelize it across sequence length. If you write the update in matrix form, the transition is identity minus beta times k k-transpose, a generalized Householder transformation, and products of those can be compactly represented with the WY representation from numerical linear algebra. That gives you a chunkwise algorithm that's hardware-friendly and uses tensor cores efficiently, so DeltaNet could finally be trained at real model sizes.

Then Gated DeltaNet combines the delta rule with a gating or decay term like in Mamba2. The two are complementary. Gating lets you quickly forget a lot of memory at once when context shifts, and the delta rule lets you do precise, targeted edits to specific associations. Together they work better than either alone, which is why you now see delta-rule-style layers in hybrid architectures in production models.

So in one sentence: the delta rule turns linear attention from a memory that only accumulates into one that can actually correct and overwrite itself, and that makes a fixed-size state far more useful.

r001.rationale: The response says beta scales the difference between the incoming target value and the value retrieved from memory, describing how much of that correction is applied.

r002.rationale: It describes writing a beta-scaled prediction error, but does not say that the error is multiplied by the key in an outer-product update.

r003.rationale: It contrasts the Delta Rule’s precise edits to specific associations with gating’s ability to forget a lot of memory at once.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I'd put it is that the Delta Rule changes how a linear attention model writes to its memory, and that turns out to be the thing that matters most.

Vanilla linear attention is purely additive. Every new key-value pair just gets summed into the state matrix. Nothing ever gets removed, so if the same key shows up again with a different value, the old association and the new one pile on top of each other. The state becomes a blurry superposition, and retrieval degrades as the context gets longer. Gating helps a little, but gating is a blunt instrument. It decays everything uniformly, or at best per channel. It can't say "forget this specific thing."

The Delta Rule is targeted. Before writing a new value, the model first reads out what the memory currently predicts for that key. Then it writes only the difference, the delta, between the new value and the old prediction. So if the association is already correct, nothing changes. If it's wrong, the old entry gets overwritten rather than accumulated alongside. Mathematically you can view it as doing one step of online gradient descent on a regression loss, so the state is actively being fit to the key-value pairs instead of just storing a running sum.

In practice that gives you much better associative recall and better in-context retrieval, which is exactly where linear attention has historically lost to softmax attention. And the thing I'm most excited about is that we showed the update can still be chunked and parallelized on hardware. The per-step update looks sequential, since each write depends on the current state, but with the right reformulation using Householder-like products you can train it efficiently on GPUs. So you keep the linear-time inference of linear attention, you get a much more expressive memory, and you don't give up training throughput. That combination is what I think makes it a real step forward rather than just a nicer equation.

r001.rationale: It describes writing the difference between the new value and the old prediction, but does not explain a beta coefficient or interpolation controlled by beta.

r002.rationale: It says the model writes the delta, but does not describe adding an outer product of that delta with the key.

r003.rationale: It contrasts targeted forgetting of a specific association with gating that decays everything uniformly or per channel.

astra-6.text:
The key improvement is that the Delta Rule lets linear attention update its memory by correcting what’s already there. Standard linear attention essentially accumulates key–value associations. That’s simple and efficient, but when you write new information, old information can interfere with it.

With the Delta Rule, you first retrieve what the memory currently predicts for a key, compare that with the value you want to store, and write back the difference. So the update is driven by a prediction error. That gives you a way to selectively overwrite an association, rather than just adding another one, while preserving the efficiency of a recurrent memory.

r001.rationale: The response describes comparing the retrieved prediction with the desired value, but does not mention a beta coefficient or interpolation controlled by it.

r002.rationale: It says the update writes back the difference, but does not specify adding an outer product of that difference with the key.

r003.rationale: It describes selectively overwriting an association, but does not distinguish targeted deletion from decay affecting multiple dimensions.

sol-6.1.text: The key improvement is that the Delta Rule lets linear attention correct its memory, rather than just keep adding to it. In standard linear attention, each new key–value pair contributes an update, and those updates can interfere with one another. With the Delta Rule, you first retrieve what the current memory predicts for the key, then update using the difference between that prediction and the new value. So you’re writing a correction into memory. That gives the model more precise control over what it stores and replaces, while preserving the efficiency of a recurrent, fixed-size state.

r001.rationale: It describes comparing the memory’s prediction with the incoming value, but does not mention a beta coefficient or its role in interpolating between them.

r002.rationale: It describes writing a correction into memory, but does not specify adding an outer product of the value difference with the key.

r003.rationale: It discusses replacing information generally, but does not distinguish targeted deletion of a memory component from broad decay.
